title: Merge, rebase, and conflict meaning
outcome: Choose a history operation from the graph and resolve intent rather than markers alone.
cue: Draw the graph before moving the label.

exercises.title: Find and fix the bug
exercises.prompt: A teammate rebased a shared branch and wants to force-push immediately. What evidence and coordination are needed?

exercises.title: Change one condition
exercises.prompt: A merge has no textual conflict but breaks an API contract. What did Git fail to prove?

trace.title: Common base
trace.detail: Merge joins histories. A merge commit can have two parents and preserve both lines of development. A fast-forward just moves a branch label when no divergent history needs joining.

trace.title: Follow the middle steps
trace.detail:
Draw O→A on main and O→B→C on your branch. Merge can produce a node with A and C as parents. Rebase builds B′ and C′ on A. The old B/C objects may still exist, but your branch now names C′.

For each conflict, read the common base, both edits, and nearby call sites. Test the combined result. Record a short explanation when the merge resolution makes a meaningful product decision.

trace.title: Check the result
trace.detail: A rebase can repeat conflicts across replayed commits. A merge can be conflict-free and still be behaviorally wrong. Git combines text; it does not understand your program’s rules.
